details:
**Symphony No. 9 in E minor, "From the New World"**
Dvořák's most famous work, written in 1893 while he was director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York. It draws on the spirit of African American and Native American music, often using pentatonic themes. It was premiered by the New York Philharmonic under Anton Seidl. It is the near-universal giveaway for him, and a recording of it is said to have been taken to the Moon by Neil Armstrong.

**Largo and the English horn solo**
The slow second movement of the New World Symphony begins with a hushed brass chorale, after which the English horn plays a famous melancholy melody in D-flat major. The movement was originally marked a faster tempo, and Dvořák changed it to Largo around the time of the premiere rehearsals.

**"Goin' Home"**
A spiritual-like song created in 1922 by Dvořák's former student William Arms Fisher, who added words to the Largo's English horn melody. It is so well known that many people mistake it for an authentic folk spiritual.

**Harry T. Burleigh and "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"**
Burleigh was an African American baritone and student at the National Conservatory who sang spirituals for Dvořák, and his voice is said to have inspired the English horn theme. A flute theme in the first movement of the New World Symphony closely resembles the spiritual "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot."

**Spillville, Iowa**
A Czech immigrant town where Dvořák spent the summer of 1893, after finishing the New World Symphony. There he wrote his "American" String Quartet and other chamber works.

**The Song of Hiawatha scherzo**
The third-movement scherzo (Molto vivace) of the New World Symphony was inspired by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem The Song of Hiawatha, specifically the wedding-feast scene with the dance of Pau-Puk-Keewis. Dvořák had also considered writing a Hiawatha opera.

**Allegro con fuoco finale**
The last movement of the New World Symphony opens with strings playing a slurred long-short half-step figure (B to C) that speeds up, often compared to John Williams's Jaws theme. Horns and trumpets then play the bold main theme in E minor, and the symphony ends with a plagal-type cadence and a final E major chord.

**"American" String Quartet (No. 12 in F major)**
Dvořák's most famous chamber work, written in Spillville in 1893. It opens with the viola playing a pentatonic melody over shimmering violins, and its third movement imitates the song of the scarlet tanager, a bird Dvořák heard in Iowa.

**Slavonic Dances**
Two sets of eight dances (Op. 46 and Op. 72), originally for piano four hands and later orchestrated. Brahms recommended Dvořák to the publisher Fritz Simrock, who commissioned the first set to follow the success of Brahms's Hungarian Dances and of Dvořák's Moravian Duets. They use Czech and Slavic folk dance forms such as the furiant, dumka, polka, and odzemek; the first set begins and ends with a furiant.

**Rusalka and the "Song to the Moon"**
Dvořák's 1901 opera about a water nymph who falls in love with a human Prince. The witch Ježibaba makes her human in exchange for her voice, while her father, the water goblin Vodník, warns against it. Her aria "Song to the Moon," in which she asks the moon to tell the Prince of her love, is his most famous vocal piece.

**Cello Concerto in B minor**
Written in 1894–95 near the end of his American stay, it is one of the most important cello concertos. Dvořák quoted his own song "Lasst mich allein" ("Leave me alone"), a favorite of his sister-in-law Josefina Čermáková, whom he had loved unrequitedly in his youth and who died while he was writing it. His early song cycle Cypresses was also inspired by her.

**Dumky Trio**
Dvořák's Piano Trio No. 4 in E minor, which breaks from standard sonata form. It consists of six dumky, a Slavic folk form that alternates between brooding, lament-like sections and sudden fast, joyful ones.

**Tone poems on Karel Jaromír Erben**
Dvořák based four late symphonic poems on Erben's Czech folk ballads: The Water Goblin (a creature who keeps the souls of drowned people under teacups), The Noon Witch, The Golden Spinning Wheel (in which the murdered Dornička is brought back to life and her wicked stepmother and stepsister are thrown to the wolves), and The Wild Dove. He also wrote the overture trilogy "Nature, Life, and Love": In Nature's Realm, Carnival, and Othello.

**Humoresque No. 7 in G-flat major**
The seventh of Dvořák's eight Humoresques for piano and his best-known piano piece, a lilting, playful tune.

**Influence on American composers**
Dvořák urged Americans to build a national style from African American and Native American music. His New World Symphony influenced Amy Beach's Gaelic Symphony and the symphonies of Florence Price and William Grant Still, and Joseph Horowitz's book Dvořák's Prophecy discusses this legacy.
